title: Gender bias and stereotypes in Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether contemporary large language models (LLMs) reproduce and amplify gender stereotypes when resolving pronouns in ambiguous sentences. The authors focus on a simple experimental paradigm built from pairs of occupations that are stereotypically male or female, paired with masculine or feminine pronouns, in order to test whether models systematically favor stereotype-consistent interpretations.

The approach is not an educational intervention; it is an evaluation of four publicly available 2023 LLMs using automatically prompted sentence-comprehension items. The models were asked to choose the referent of a pronoun in ambiguous sentences and then, in a follow-up, to indicate whether the other noun could also be a referent. The paper also includes a baseline with names added to disambiguate the pronoun and compares model choices against both human stereotype ratings and U.S. labor statistics.

The study does not involve human participants, students, teachers, or a school setting. It finds that the models strongly align pronoun resolution with gender stereotypes, often fail to acknowledge ambiguity unless explicitly asked, and provide explanations that can be factually inaccurate or rationalize biased choices. The authors conclude that LLMs reflect and sometimes amplify societal gender bias, and argue that such systems should be carefully evaluated for harms before deployment in high-impact domains, including education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models / generative AI chatbots that produce and interpret natural language text.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates four publicly available LLMs on gender bias in pronoun resolution and on how they explain their choices.

findings.finding_summary: Across four LLMs, the models showed strong gender-stereotyped pronoun resolution: stereotypically female occupations were chosen more often with feminine pronouns and stereotypically male occupations with masculine pronouns. The paper reports that models were on average 6.8 times more likely to choose a stereotypically female occupation when a female pronoun was present and 3.4 times more likely to choose a stereotypically male occupation when a male pronoun was present; the sentences were noted as ambiguous only 5% of the time.
findings.measure: Occupation choice in ambiguous pronoun-resolution prompts; ambiguity acknowledgement

findings.finding_summary: When explicit gendered names were added to disambiguate the sentences, the models largely resolved the pronouns correctly even when this contradicted gender stereotypes. Accuracy on these baseline items was very high across models: 98%, 99%, 97%, and 99% respectively, indicating the models could use explicit information to override stereotypical expectations.

The models’ occupation choices tracked perceived gender stereotypes more closely than labor-market ground truth. Reported Kendall’s τ correlations were τ=0.67 vs τ=0.5 for human ratings vs BLS statistics for the masculine pronoun, and τ=0.49 vs τ=0.46 for the feminine pronoun; all p-values were < 0.001. The paper also reports that stereotypes about women were amplified more than those about men.
findings.measure: Kendall’s tau correlation between model choices and perceived occupation gender association vs BLS statistics

findings.finding_summary: Three of the four models usually acknowledged ambiguity only when explicitly asked, while initially giving categorical answers. On the follow-up question about whether the other noun could also be the referent, the models answered yes at rates of 64%, 82%, 26%, and 85% respectively, but one model mostly insisted its original answer was the only possible one.
findings.measure: Explicit acknowledgment that sentence was ambiguous

findings.finding_summary: The paper finds that the models often produced explanations that were factually inaccurate or rationalized biased choices after the fact. Grammar-based explanations accounted for over 20% of explanations, and explicitly gender-biased explanations were given about 5-15% of the time; however, the study does not report a single pooled numerical effect size beyond these proportions.
findings.measure: Type and frequency of generated explanations

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, original correlational evaluation of four LLMs with manually coded outputs rather than an experiment on learners. The methodology is clear, but it does not test educational outcomes and provides no causal evidence for K-12 literacy effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s findings concern bias, ambiguity handling, and explanation quality in LLMs, not student learning gains or losses. It is relevant to downstream educational use, but the direct instructional impact is unclear and not quantified for K-12 literacy.
